summary: Discusses the URI resolution services needed to resolve Uniform Resource Names, going beyond simply retrieving a resource. Examples include getting aliases or a description of the resource. It is an experimental specification.

plainLanguage.summary: A URI (Uniform Resource Identifier) can be used for more than fetching a file. A client may want to know where the resource lives, what else it is called, or what it is. RFC 2483 gives these requests short names, so a client asks for exactly the one it wants and a server offers only the ones it supports. It also defines a simple text format for answering with a list of URIs.

questions: what services are needed to resolve urns
what is i2l in urn resolution

what operations are defined for uri resolution
subtitle: Nine named operations for asking a server what a URI means, beyond just fetching the resource.

tldr.problem: Retrieving the resource a URI names is only one of the things a client might want to do with it, and no single server can be expected to support every possible function.
tldr.mechanism: The memo names nine operations, from I2L (URI to URL) to I=I (URI equal to URI), and states what each one must declare: its operands, its algorithm, its output and its errors. It also registers the text/uri-list media type for answers that are lists of URIs.
tldr.outcome: Because the request names the operation, a client can find a server that specialises in the function it needs and a server can say which functions it offers. The document is Experimental.

facts.label: Operations defined
facts.value: 9 (I2L, I2Ls, I2R, I2Rs, I2C, I2Cs, I2N, I2Ns, I=I)

today: RFC 2483 is an Experimental document that has not been obsoleted or updated. The memo anticipates that the set of named operations would grow and that a registration mechanism would then be needed, but it does not define one.

sections.title: Why the Operations Were Named
sections.content:
RFC 2483 grew out of work on URNs (Uniform Resource Names). The authors found that asking servers to implement every useful function was unrealistic, and so was asking clients to make sense of whatever a server happened to return. Both slowed down adoption. What a client needed was a way to tell a server that specialises in the complicated work from one that specialises in the simple, fast work.

Some operations also turned out to be inappropriate or difficult for certain identifiers. A design criterion was therefore kept deliberately small: name the operation with a short token, and state its operands, its algorithm and its errors. Earlier versions of the document used names tied to one kind of identifier, such as N2L and L2L; those were replaced by the more general URI forms used here.

The memo also draws a line around Uniform Resource Characteristics (URCs). They appear in the document as descriptions of resources, never as identifiers in their own right.
sections.plainLanguage: A URI can be used for more than fetching a file, and different servers are good at different jobs. This memo gives the common requests short names so a client can ask for the one it needs. It also keeps descriptions of a resource separate from names for it.

sections.title: What Each Operation Must Specify
sections.content:
Any document that defines a new operation has to state its operands, its algorithm, its output and its errors. The operands must give the name of the operation, a mnemonic for it that does not depend on letter case, the number of operands, the type of each operand and the format of each operand.

The algorithm must either be written out in full or be treated as opaque and left to the server or the application. The output must be described as one of a small set of cases: there is no output, the output is undefined, the output itself together with its content, the fact that the output is an object together with that object's type and format, or any errors that are not specific to the protocol.

Error conditions must cover every error that applies across all implementations and application environments. Errors that depend on the system carrying the service are left out, so service availability and the syntax of the operation itself are not in the document because they are implementation dependent. Each operation must also describe its own security considerations, but not the protocol used to convey the service nor the results of the service themselves.

Because the list of functions is short, the memo treats a registration mechanism as premature, and says one will probably be needed if the list grows. It also uses the RFC 2119 words sparingly: where they appear, they mark cases where this specification could cause harm to existing, non-experimental systems such as HTTP and URNs.
sections.plainLanguage: Every named operation has to say four things: what it takes as input, how it works, what it gives back, and what can go wrong. The document also sets a limit on the errors each operation lists. Errors that depend on the particular system carrying the service are left out.

sections.title: Encoding the Operations in a Protocol
sections.content:
The operations only become useful once they travel inside some system or protocol, and each such system restricts which operations make sense and how they are written down. A protocol is free to define new operations inside its own specification document, but it should make the fact well known.

A protocol also has its own rules about output, and may encode results better than the general case the memo describes. As an example, the result of an operation that turns one URI into several URLs might be encoded in a protocol-specific way that also conveys how close each of those URLs is on the network.

Four things have to be settled for any protocol that carries these operations: which subset of the operations is allowed, how the operation is encoded, how the operands are encoded, and how error codes are returned. The text/uri-list media type in the next section is offered as a suggestion for experimental systems that want a simple implementation, included to show completeness.
sections.plainLanguage: Each protocol that carries these requests decides four things for itself: which requests it allows, how a request is written, how the URI is written, and how errors come back. The media type in the next section is one simple example of such an encoding.

sections.title: The Incomplete Set of Operations
sections.content:
The memo lists nine operations, each with one or two URI operands, an opaque algorithm and a defined output. I2L returns one and only one URL. I2Ls returns a list of zero or more URLs, and the client is told not to assume any order. I2R returns a single instance of the resource named by the URI. I2Rs returns zero or more instances, for example a GIF and a JPEG of the same image; its output shall be a MIME multipart/alternative message with the alternative versions in separate body parts, though it may be sent without that wrapper when only one version exists.

I2C returns a URC, a description of the resource, which might be a bibliographic citation, a digital signature or a revision history. The memo does not specify the content of a URC response, because that content is expected to vary from one server to another. I2Cs returns zero or more URCs. I2N returns one and only one URN naming the same resource, and I2Ns returns a list of them.

The memo warns about I2N. URNs are meant to identify one and only one resource, but a resource may have more than one name, so two organisations can agree that the names 'foo' and 'bar' stand for the same thing. Equality is domain specific: a URN pointing to a weather map for a particular day and a URN pointing to that map as it changes from day to day would not be equivalent. The last operation, I=I, takes two URIs and answers TRUE or FALSE, using an opaque algorithm and making no claim about whether the URIs behave like URNs or like URLs.

The errors listed for the one-operand operations are the same throughout: a malformed URI; a syntactically valid URI that does not exist in any form; a URI that exists but has no output available from this operation; a URI that existed in the past but about which nothing is currently known; and access denied.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo names nine requests, such as URI to URL and URI to description. Each one takes a URI and says what comes back: one URL, a list of URLs, the resource itself, or a description of it. The set is called incomplete because more could be added later.

sections.title: The text/uri-list Media Type
sections.content:
Several of the operations, I2Ls and I2Ns among them, produce a list of URIs. The text/uri-list media type gives a simple format for those lists, intended for automatic processing rather than for people to read. The section is a copy of the IANA registration.

The rules are short. Lines beginning with a hash character are comment lines and are ignored, and because URIs may themselves contain a hash, that character only starts a comment when it is the first character on a line. The remaining lines shall be URIs, one URI per line, and very long URIs are not broken across lines. As for all text/* formats, lines are terminated with a CRLF pair.

When one URI has been mapped to a list of URIs, the first line of the response should be a comment giving the original URI. The registration recommends the file extensions .uris or .uri, lists intended usage as Limited Use, and notes that URN resolvers are the first applications of the format, with web clients and proxies named as likely later users.
sections.plainLanguage: The media type is a plain text list, one URI per line, with lines starting with a hash treated as comments. It exists so that a program can read the answer automatically. A server answering with a list should name the original URI in the first comment line.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Communications with a resolver may be of a sensitive nature. Some servers hold information that should only be released to authorised users, so the results a server returns may be the target of spoofing, and the requests themselves may be of interest to traffic analysts. The requests may also be subject to spoofing.

The Access denied error assumes a system that can convey an authenticated notion of access control, so it should only be returned by systems that have a method of determining access control.

Two concerns recur under every operation: malicious redirection, where a bad entry in a resolver's database sends clients to the wrong URL, and denial of service, where removing the URL removes the client's ability to retrieve the resource at all. The text/uri-list registration adds that the lookup and reverse lookup potential of a URI list may attract traffic analysts, and that such lists may reveal confidential information such as the location of sensitive information, so confidentiality measures should be available to protect uri-list responses when appropriate.
sections.plainLanguage: A resolver may hold information meant only for some users, so the answers and the questions can both be worth attacking or watching. The document lists the same two worries for every operation: a resolver that sends clients to the wrong place, and a resolver whose entry is removed so the resource cannot be fetched.

items.label: URI to URLs
items.desc: A list of zero or more URLs.

items.label: URI to Resource
items.desc: An instance of the resource named by the URI.

items.label: URI to Resources
items.desc: Zero or more instances of the resource.

items.label: URI to URCs
items.desc: Zero or more descriptions of the resource.

items.label: URI to URN
items.desc: One and only one URN naming the same resource.
